doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Parents, school music, trumpet and cousin Dick Schaap
summary: His mother's violin demand, the school music program, his memory, and cousin Dick Schaap's tickets and Billy Crystal ties.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I see. Were your parents thrilled that you were getting this?
Yes. No. My mother was eventually thrilled. She was fighting the sports and music thing. I mean her idea was — I wanted to learn an instrument and it was violin or nothing so I said nothing.

Yeah. She may not — I may be making her out to be more shrewish, she was a zany Bohemian jazz lover. But she didn’t want — I guess she wanted the best for me and she had to figure out what the best was at the time. So I got involved in singing with my boy soprano in the major music program of the New York City public school system which was an excellent program in those days. Always yearning to be in the instrumental

program and the enriched program — they call it SPE — or they called it I gather, I have no idea whether it still exists in the New York City public school system. But SPE is a special program for good, gifted students. But the E meant there’d be some music component. Enriched is what it stood for. And you either went into the band or you went into the chorus. And I wanted that band bad. But I’d been singing on an enriched music program with this boy soprano fourth, fifth and sixth grade because I had done okay on the recorder class, they give you some recorder lessons and I did okay, so and then I passed some listening test which probably I shouldn’t have passed because I’m not that good. And they wouldn’t let me take an instrument. So I started studying trumpet on the side on my own in adolescence. But my mother, my grandfather, her father, was an excellent musician, an organist, a church organist, but he was a lawyer. And my father’s father was a lawyer. And lawyer — they discovered this memory, you know when I was two I could do the presidents, forward and backward, with their dates. I still can do it but I do it slower than I did in 1953. And it’s not just because there are more presidents since Truman, it’s that some of them are more forgettable than Truman. And you know so she wanted that. And I loved those Brooklyn Dodgers and — “You don’t take my son to baseball games” she really didn’t want me to go to the sports things. And fortunately for me if thwarting that is important, was that my illustrious cousin, you know, hit big time sports right then and started like free ticket city. That would be Dick Schaap. He died just slightly more than a year ago. And he went with Newsweek and Sport Magazine right around the time I entered elementary school and the next, until he was city editor of the Herald Tribune which would be like ’63 or ‘4, it was sports heaven in a Schaap house, any Schaap household. I mean what does Billy Crystal say? They’re pretty tight, Billy Crystal and my late cousin were very tight, he says, “What is the first thing you think of when you think of Dick Schaap?” “Tickets.” And boy he wasn’t in the family. And it’s funny, you know during that time I knew Billy Crystal’s father. He stunned — I mean Billy Crystal is close friends of this area of our family, the Schaap family, they are tight. But I knew Jack Crystal and Bernhardt Crystal, Jack’s brother, who still lives. And I’ve only met Billy Crystal and spoken with him largely about his father. And I actually have something that Billy Crystal wants from me. I have — Jack Crystal used to let me into the Central Plaza for cheap. I don’t think he let me in for free, but he let me in for cheap. And Billy Crystal said, “Did you save the ticket stubs?” And my mother was half pack rat and half insane throw outer. So the autograph collection and the programs, my Scotty LaFaro autograph and all the others, it’s gone. But one ticket stub, I must have put it in the wrong place, from the Central Plaza. And he wants the Central Plaza ticket stub.
